title: The Great Exhibition

paragraphs.text: If you had taken an omnibus through London’s Knightsbridge in the summer of 1851, you would have witnessed an astonishing sight. Glittering among the trees was a palace made of glass, like something out of the Arabian Nights’ Recent rainfall had washed the dust from the glass, and made it glitter all the more. Nothing like this had ever been seen before in London. This building, called the ‘Crystal Palace’, housed the ‘Great Exhibition of the Works of industry of All Nations’. The Great Exhibition was the idea of Queen Victoria’s husband, Prince Albert. Britain was at peace, both at home and abroad. This was the time to show off, on the international stage.

There were some 100,000 objects at the exhibition, by over 15,000 contributors. Britain, as host, occupied half the display space inside, with exhibits from both Britain and the British Empire. The remaining space was occupied by items from all over the world. The British exhibits included adding machines which could accurately do the work of a bank clerk. There was a printing machine that could turn out 5,000 copies of the popular periodical the Illustrated London News in an hour, and another for printing and folding envelopes. There was an invention based on rubber tubes to help the deaf to hear, and ‘tangible ink for the blind, which produced raised characters on paper. The biggest exhibit of all was the massive hydraulic press that had lifted the metal tubes of a bridge in Wales. Each tube weighed 1,144 tons, yet just one man was required to operate the press. Next in size was a steam hammer that could, with equal accuracy, shape the main bearing of a steamship or gently crack an egg. A whole gallery was devoted to the elegant, sophisticated carriages that predated the motorcar, and one or two velocipedes, the early version of bicycles. There were printing presses and textile machines and agricultural machines: As the Queen wrote in her diary, there was ‘every conceivable invention’.

Canada sent a fire engine with painted panels showing Canadian scenes, and a collection of furs. India contributed an elaborate throne of carved ivory, a coat embroidered with pearls, emeralds and rubies. and a magnificent canopied seat for a rajah’s elephant. A massive eagle, wings outstretched and holding the national flag, stood above the exhibits from the USA. Although the general idea of the Exhibition was the promotion of world peace, Colt’s repeating fire-arms featured prominently beneath the flag, but so did McCormick’s machine for gathering crops.

The largest foreign contributor was France. its exhibits included magnificent tapestries and silk drapes. Unlike British exhibits of the same type, many of which were sadly lacking in taste, the visual impact of the French display was stunning. It was backed up by examples of the machinery used to produce these beautiful objects. The Russian exhibits were late. having been held up by ice in the Baltic Sea. When they did arrive, they were wonderful.
They included massive vases made of porcelain, a piece of malachite’ twice the height of a man, an assortment of sledges, and a suit of Cossack armour.

Among all these wonders, there was one which particularly caught the public imagination: the famous Koh-i-Noor diamond, it was supposed to be of inestimable value, but although people crowded round to see it, most found it disappointing. It lay in a secure cage, and although on special days it was lit by a dozen little gas jets, it still failed to sparkle. It was not until later, when it had been skilfully cut, that its beauty emerged.

The building itself, designed by Joseph Paxton, was the most breathtaking exhibit of all. Paxton’s innovative design used modules of glass and iron, that could be fabricated off site, put in place and in due course taken apart again, since the building was only to be temporary: Work had begun on 1 August 1850. By December 1850, more than 2,000 men were working on the side. By means of ingenious machines invented by Paxton’s team, these machines were intended to clean the glass automatically, in practice the trailing skirts of the women visitors did this job splendidly. Inside, the famous fountain, standing approximately in the middle of the building, was made of four tons of pink glass. it provided a useful meeting place, as well as cooling the atmosphere. There was a police desk for lost children and there were various areas where light refreshments were available. And for the first time ever at an exhibition. waiting rooms and toilets were provided.

Queen Victoria opened the Exhibition on 1 May in 1851, on schedule. She became a frequent visitor. At first the price of admission was £3 for gentlemen, £2 for ladies. From 24 May, the masses were let in for only a shilling a head. And they came in their thousands, factory workers sent by their employers, villagers sent by benevolent landowners, and strings of schoolchildren. By the time the Exhibition closed on 11 October, over six million people had gone through the turnstiles.

questions.prompt: A minority of exhibition visitors went to look at the Koh-i-Noor.
An effort was made to improve the way the Koh-i-Noor was displayed.
The modules used to construct the exhibition building were later re-assembled elsewhere.
Construction work on the exhibition building progressed at a slow pace.

A glass fountain helped maintain a comfortable air temperature.
